catalog_quote: Based on the relative pitch level, tone in Gua exhibits two basic forms. The basic tone levels are low and high. ... Gua is a register tone language which makes use of the height of the pitch to distinguish words. As a register tone language, Gua tones are expected to be realised on relative low and high level pitches. However, it is possible to realise low-high or high-low level pitches (especially on disyllabic words), which are referred to as rising and falling pitches respectively. ... 4.5.1 Lexical Function of Tone in Gua As noted above, lexical function of tone indicates how the meanings of two or more segmentally identical words are distinguished depending on the tone patterns on the words. ... 109. kú hole / kù cut/dig 110. lʊ́ hernia / lʊ̀ weave ... 113. ɲɛ́ name / ɲɛ̀ get

tone_statements.quote: Anum is a two-tone Kwa language spoken in Ghana. It belongs to the Guang branch of the Kwa languages, which branches into the North, North-East, Central, and South Guang languages; Anum belongs to the South Guang languages (also called Gwa) (Kropp Dakubu 1988, p. 79). … Although Anum is a tone language, I have refrained from giving the tonal transcription since lexical tone does not play a role in RVH.
tone_statements.locator: p. 1 of 28, sec. 1 Introduction and p. 6 of 28, sec. 3.1 Speech Materials
tone_statements.summary: Called a two-tone language with lexical tone; units not characterised (never named as high/low or as contours, no tonal transcription or analysis given; the study concerns ATR vowel harmony).

Elugbe (eds.), Language typology and language documentation in West Africa: proceedings of the 27th West African Linguistics Congress (WALS). Paris: L'Harmattan'.
tone_statements.quote: Gua has 2 basic level tones: low (L) and high (H). The tone bearing unit (TBU) is the mora. Example (1) shows level tone distinctions between verbs and nouns in monomoraic words. The verbs have L tone while the nouns have H tone. … Falling (HL) tone occurs on some nouns as illustrated in (2). This happens on the final vowel of bimoraic nouns. … There are contour tones on verbs with diphthongs and long vowels. Yip (2002) notes that rising and falling tones result from the combination of two level tones. This appears to be the case in Gua. … Gua tone on verbs has only grammatical functions.
tone_statements.locator: p. 3, sec. 2.0 'Basic Tone in Gua', plus first sentence of sec. 3.0 (pp. 3-4)
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, high and low, borne by the mora; falling and rising are H+L sequences over two moras. Verbs have no lexical tone: TMA melodies L, HL, LH spread right-to-left, with polar prefixes.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated sections/pages in the 2013 thesis text we hold. The classification (tonal; two level tones H/L, downstep; no word stress described; domain not stated by the source) rests on a dedicated phonology thesis and is now independently confirmed by the author's 2021 UCSD PhD dissertation (downloaded, Ch.7 pp.206-261), which is the best available description per Glottolog; it refines only the TBU (mora, not syllable), which does not touch any coded field. No other stress/prosody source for Gua exists in Glottolog or Crossref. Optional housekeeping only: add Obiri-Yeboah 2021 sec. 7.1 p.207 as a corroborating citation in refs/sources; no reclassification.

sources.citation: Obiri-Yeboah, Michael. 2021. Phonetics and Phonology of Gua. PhD dissertation, University of California San Diego. xvii+284 pp. eScholarship qt6tx034q1.
sources.quote: p.207: 'Gua has two basic level tones: low (L) and high (H), with downstep. ... The tone bearing unit (TBU) is the mora.' p.206: 'Tone has a lexical function in nouns, adjectives and postpositions. However, in the verbal system, Gua has grammatical tone that can be analyzed as tone melodies (systematic tone patterns) L, LH and HL which are exponents of the Tense, Aspect and Mood (TAM) system.' p.260: 'the language uses tone to mark lexical and grammatical structures.' No word stress or accent is posited anywhere; 'stress'/'prominence' occur only in cross-linguistic asides (fn.21 p.93 on promin

sources.note: Top-ranked Glottolog description (full phonetics+phonology PhD, 284 pp, with a 55-page tonology chapter) superseding the 2013 M.Phil thesis our classification rests on; now obtained and read, confirms tonal with no stress system.
